title: Give them time to think
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino argues that checking for understanding immediately after new information is presented often fails not because students weren't attending, but because they haven't had time to process what they just attended to. She distinguishes genuine attention from its illusion: students can look focused while their minds have wandered, and even a genuinely attentive student often struggles to explain back something they could recognise moments earlier, because they haven't had a chance to mentally manipulate what they heard. Castelino illustrates the fix with a paired classroom example teaching how nerve impulses cross a synapse: in the unmodified version, she moves straight from explanation to quizzing and gets patchy recall; in the modified version, she inserts a minute or two of silent thinking time, sometimes paired rehearsal, before repeating the explanation a second time and only then checking understanding. The second explanation, she argues, does double duty -- students who have already tried to process the material can now use it to identify and fill their own gaps rather than hearing the same content passively twice. She closes by acknowledging the technique costs lesson time, but argues it is worth the investment for key concepts that later content depends on, since it leaves students with a more secure foundation than rushing straight to questions.
points: Castelino distinguishes the illusion of attention (looking focused) from genuine processing, arguing that even attentive students often can't explain back new material without time to mentally manipulate it first.

Her paired classroom example (teaching the synapse) shows immediate quizzing after explanation producing patchy recall, versus inserting silent thinking time and a second explanation before quizzing producing stronger recall days later.

The second explanation does double duty: students who have already tried to process the material can use it to identify and fill their own specific gaps, rather than simply hearing the same content passively twice.
Castelino explicitly costs the technique in lesson time and argues it is worth the trade-off specifically for key concepts that later content depends on, not for every piece of new information.
quotes: Recently, a lot of attention has been placed on attention (#sorrynotsorry).
Part of this may very well be because there is simply an illusion of attention. They look like they are focused but they are thinking about football or what they will have for lunch.
One small change I have made to my own teaching is to give my students time to think about what they have just heard.
Once students have had the chance to think and write about a concept, a second explanation helps them identify gaps in their knowledge.
A few days later, I pose questions on the synapse and more students can confidently tell me what happens.
However, when it comes to key concepts that several other content is built upon, using this technique means students have a stronger foundation than if we just rush through teaching it all.
